questions.stem: In a Cisco SD-Access fabric, which component is responsible for the control-plane mapping of endpoint IDs (EIDs) to routing locators (RLOCs)?

explanation.correct: SD-Access uses LISP for the control plane. The control-plane node acts as the LISP Map-Server/Map-Resolver, holding the EID-to-RLOC mappings that edge nodes query to reach endpoints.

distractors.A: Edge nodes register and query EIDs but do not hold the authoritative map database themselves.
distractors.C: Border nodes connect the fabric to external networks (the 'exit'), not the EID map.
distractors.D: The WLC integrates wireless into the fabric but is not the LISP control plane.

explanation.exam_pattern: SD-Access planes: LISP=control (map-server/resolver), VXLAN=data plane, Cisco TrustSec/SGT=policy. Match the node role: edge=endpoints, border=exit, control=LISP DB.

questions.stem: Two Catalyst switches are combined so they appear as a single logical switch with one control plane, allowing a downstream device to form a single cross-chassis EtherChannel. Which technology is this?

explanation.correct: StackWise Virtual (and VSS on older platforms) merges two chassis into one logical switch with a single control plane, enabling a Multichassis EtherChannel (MEC) and removing the need for STP blocking on the uplinks.

distractors.B: HSRP is a first-hop gateway redundancy protocol; each switch keeps its own control plane.
distractors.C: VRRP is also an FHRP (IETF standard), not a chassis-virtualization technology.
distractors.D: GLBP is an FHRP that load-balances gateways; it does not merge control planes.

explanation.exam_pattern: StackWise Virtual/VSS = one logical device + MEC. FHRPs (HSRP/VRRP/GLBP) = separate devices sharing a virtual gateway. Don't confuse chassis virtualization with gateway redundancy.

questions.stem: An AP is configured in FlexConnect mode at a branch. The CAPWAP tunnel to the central WLC goes down. What happens to clients on a locally-switched WLAN?

options.text: All clients immediately disconnect because the WLC is unreachable
Locally-switched clients keep forwarding traffic locally (standalone mode)
The AP reboots and joins the nearest AP as a mesh node
Traffic is tunneled to a backup WLC over the Internet automatically

explanation.correct: FlexConnect allows local switching of WLAN traffic at the branch. If the WAN/CAPWAP to the WLC fails, the AP enters standalone mode and continues switching already-authenticated clients locally.

distractors.A: That describes centrally-switched (local-mode) behaviour, not FlexConnect local switching.
distractors.C: FlexConnect APs do not convert to mesh nodes on WLC loss.
distractors.D: There is no automatic Internet-tunneled backup WLC behaviour implied here.

explanation.exam_pattern: FlexConnect = branch APs, local switching + survivability (standalone on WAN loss). Local mode = all traffic tunneled to WLC (central switching).

questions.stem: In a three-tier campus design, which layer's primary job is fast, high-capacity transport and interconnecting distribution blocks — with no policy, filtering, or CPU-intensive features?

explanation.correct: The core is built for speed and resilience — it switches packets between distribution blocks as fast as possible and avoids anything that adds latency (ACLs, policy, redistribution).

distractors.A: The access layer connects endpoints and applies port security, PoE, VLANs.
distractors.B: The distribution layer is where routing/policy/filtering/aggregation live.
distractors.D: The WAN/edge layer handles external connectivity, not intra-campus core transport.

explanation.exam_pattern: Access=connect endpoints, Distribution=aggregate+policy/routing, Core=fast transport (keep it simple). Policy belongs at distribution, not core.

questions.stem: Which first-hop redundancy protocol natively load-balances traffic across multiple active gateways by handing out different virtual MAC addresses in ARP replies?

explanation.correct: GLBP (Gateway Load Balancing Protocol) uses one AVG that replies to ARP with different virtual MACs for up to four AVFs, so hosts spread their traffic across multiple active gateways automatically.

distractors.A: HSRP has one active and one standby — only the active forwards (no native per-flow balancing without multiple groups).
distractors.B: VRRP similarly has one master forwarding at a time.
distractors.D: StackWise is chassis stacking, not an FHRP.

explanation.exam_pattern: GLBP = Cisco, load-balances via multiple vMACs (AVG/AVF). HSRP/VRRP = active/standby (balance only by using multiple groups). GLBP and HSRP are Cisco; VRRP is the open standard.

questions.stem: VXLAN is used as the data-plane encapsulation in modern fabrics. Which statement about VXLAN is correct?

options.text: It adds a 24-bit VNI, allowing ~16 million segments, and encapsulates in UDP
It adds a 12-bit VLAN ID, allowing 4094 segments, over TCP
It is a Layer 2 protocol that cannot traverse a routed underlay
It replaces IP entirely in the underlay

explanation.correct: VXLAN uses a 24-bit VXLAN Network Identifier (VNI) for ~16M segments and encapsulates Ethernet frames in UDP (dest port 4789), so it tunnels L2 over a routed L3 underlay (MAC-in-UDP).

distractors.B: The 12-bit 4094-segment limit is exactly the 802.1Q VLAN constraint VXLAN was designed to overcome; VXLAN uses UDP, not TCP.
distractors.C: VXLAN's whole point is to extend L2 ACROSS a routed L3 underlay.
distractors.D: VXLAN runs ON TOP of an IP underlay; it does not replace IP.

explanation.exam_pattern: VXLAN = 24-bit VNI (16M), MAC-in-UDP port 4789, L2-over-L3. Contrast with 802.1Q's 12-bit/4094 limit. Often paired with BGP EVPN as the control plane.

questions.stem: You configure VRF-Lite to separate two customers' routing on one router. Which command associates interface Gi0/1 with the customer VRF named RED?

options.text: ip vrf forwarding RED (under interface Gi0/1)

explanation.correct: Under the interface, 'vrf forwarding RED' (or legacy 'ip vrf forwarding RED') binds the interface to the VRF. The VRF itself is created globally with 'vrf definition RED'.

distractors.B: 'vrf definition RED' creates the VRF in global config; it is not the interface-binding command.
distractors.C: 'ip route vrf RED ...' adds a static route in the VRF table, not an interface assignment.
distractors.D: There is no 'switchport vrf' command; VRF binding is a Layer 3 interface concept.

explanation.exam_pattern: Two steps: (1) 'vrf definition NAME' globally, (2) 'vrf forwarding NAME' on the interface. Assigning the VRF clears any existing IP — readd the address after.

questions.stem: Which hypervisor type runs directly on the physical hardware without a host operating system underneath it?

explanation.correct: A Type 1 'bare-metal' hypervisor (ESXi, Hyper-V, KVM) installs directly on hardware for best performance and is standard in data centers.

distractors.B: Type 2 hypervisors run as an application ON an existing OS (desktop virtualization).
distractors.C: Containers share the host OS kernel and are not hypervisors at all.
distractors.D: There is no standard 'Type 3' hypervisor category.

explanation.exam_pattern: Type 1 = on hardware (ESXi/KVM/Hyper-V). Type 2 = on an OS (VirtualBox/VMware Workstation). Containers ≠ VMs (shared kernel).

questions.stem: Which tunneling technology lets you carry multiple protocols and multicast across an IP core by encapsulating them in IP, but provides NO encryption by itself?

explanation.correct: GRE encapsulates arbitrary protocols (and supports multicast) in IP but offers no confidentiality — which is why it is frequently paired with IPsec (GRE over IPsec) when security is needed.

distractors.B: IPsec ESP encrypts but, in tunnel mode alone, does not natively carry multicast/multiprotocol the way GRE does.
distractors.C: MACsec (802.1AE) encrypts at Layer 2 on a link, not a multiprotocol IP tunnel.
distractors.D: TLS secures application sessions, not a multiprotocol network tunnel.

explanation.exam_pattern: GRE = flexible/multicast-capable, NO encryption. Need security → GRE over IPsec. MACsec = L2 hop encryption. The 'no encryption' clue points to GRE.

verify_cli: show ip interface brief | include Tunnel

questions.stem: In a BGP EVPN VXLAN fabric, what is the role of BGP EVPN (the control plane)?

options.text: It encapsulates user frames into UDP for transport
It advertises MAC/IP reachability (and VTEP info) so flooding is minimized
It replaces the IP underlay routing protocol
It assigns IP addresses to endpoints via DHCP

explanation.correct: BGP EVPN distributes endpoint MAC/IP-to-VTEP reachability (Type-2 routes) and VTEP/VNI membership (Type-3), enabling control-plane learning that cuts down the flood-and-learn behaviour of data-plane-only VXLAN.

distractors.A: Encapsulation into UDP is VXLAN's DATA plane, not EVPN's control-plane job.
distractors.C: An IGP (OSPF/IS-IS) still provides underlay reachability for the VTEPs; EVPN rides on top.
distractors.D: EVPN does not perform DHCP address assignment.

explanation.exam_pattern: VXLAN = data plane (encap). BGP EVPN = control plane (MAC/IP advertisement, reduces flooding). Underlay IGP still needed for VTEP reachability.

questions.stem: A router has two eBGP paths to the same prefix, identical in weight, local-preference, AS-path length, origin, and MED. Which attribute is evaluated NEXT in the BGP best-path algorithm?

options.text: Prefer the path learned via eBGP over iBGP
Prefer the path with the highest MED

explanation.correct: After weight, local-pref, locally-originated, AS-path, origin, and MED, the next tiebreak is to prefer eBGP paths over iBGP paths.

distractors.B: Lowest (not highest) router-id is used, and only much later in the list after IGP metric and the oldest-eBGP check.
distractors.C: Oldest eBGP path is a later tiebreaker, after the eBGP-over-iBGP step.
distractors.D: BGP prefers the LOWEST MED, and MED was already stated to be equal here.

explanation.exam_pattern: Order mnemonic: We Love Oranges AS Oranges Mean Pure Refreshment (Weight, Local-pref, Originate/self, AS-path, Origin, MED, eBGP>iBGP, IGP metric, oldest, Router-ID, neighbor IP). Lowest MED wins.

questions.stem: Which OSPF LSA type is generated by an ABR to describe networks in one area to other areas (inter-area routes)?

explanation.correct: Type 3 Summary LSAs are originated by Area Border Routers to advertise prefixes from one area into another (inter-area/O IA routes).

distractors.A: Type 1 Router LSAs are flooded WITHIN an area, describing a router's links.
distractors.B: Type 2 Network LSAs are generated by the DR on multiaccess segments, within an area.
distractors.D: Type 5 External LSAs are generated by an ASBR for routes redistributed from outside OSPF (O E1/E2).

explanation.exam_pattern: Type 1=router(intra), 2=network(DR), 3=ABR summary(inter-area), 4=ASBR locator, 5=ASBR external, 7=NSSA external. ABR→Type 3, ASBR→Type 5.

questions.stem: In EIGRP, a route's successor has a feasible distance (FD) of 3072. A neighbor advertises the same prefix with a reported distance (RD) of 2560. Does that neighbor qualify as a feasible successor?

options.text: Yes — its RD (2560) is less than the successor's FD (3072), meeting the feasibility condition
No — its RD must be greater than the FD to be loop-free
Yes — any neighbor is automatically a feasible successor
No — feasible successors require an equal FD

explanation.correct: The Feasibility Condition: a neighbor is a feasible successor if its Reported Distance is LESS than the current successor's Feasible Distance. 2560 < 3072, so it qualifies as a loop-free backup.

distractors.B: That is backwards — RD must be LESS than FD (RD < FD) to guarantee loop-free.
distractors.C: Not every neighbor qualifies; only those meeting the feasibility condition.
distractors.D: Feasible successors do not need an equal FD; they need RD < FD.

explanation.exam_pattern: Feasibility Condition: RD(neighbor) < FD(successor) → feasible successor (instant backup, no recomputation). Otherwise DUAL goes active.

questions.stem: An EtherChannel's members pass traffic for many flows, but one high-volume server conversation is not balancing across links. Which change is MOST likely to improve link utilization?

options.text: Change the load-balancing hash to include Layer 4 ports (src-dst-port)
Add more VLANs to the trunk
Switch from LACP to static 'on' mode
Lower the STP priority of the port-channel

explanation.correct: EtherChannel hashes each flow to ONE member link. A single src/dst IP pair always hashes the same way; adding Layer 4 ports (src-dst-port) to the hash gives more entropy so sub-flows spread across members.

distractors.B: Adding VLANs does not change how a single conversation is hashed.
distractors.C: Static 'on' does not change load-balancing behaviour; the hash algorithm does.
distractors.D: STP priority affects root/forwarding, not intra-bundle load distribution.

explanation.exam_pattern: EtherChannel never splits a single flow — it balances per-flow via a hash. More hash inputs (add L4 ports, or src-dst vs dst-only) = better spread. Set with 'port-channel load-balance'.

questions.stem: In PIM Sparse Mode, what does the notation (*, G) represent in the multicast routing table?

options.text: A source-specific tree rooted at a particular source for group G
A shared tree for group G rooted at the Rendezvous Point, for any source
A unicast route to the group's gateway

explanation.correct: (*, G) is the shared tree entry for group G rooted at the RP; the '*' means 'any source'. Receivers first join the shared tree toward the RP, then may switch to a source tree (S, G).

distractors.A: A source-specific tree is written (S, G), with a specific source S.
distractors.C: Multicast state is not a unicast route; (*, G) is group forwarding state.
distractors.D: (*, G) includes incoming interface and an outgoing interface LIST, not just prunes.

explanation.exam_pattern: (*, G) = shared tree via RP (any source). (S, G) = shortest-path/source tree. PIM-SM joins shared first, then may SPT-switch to (S, G).

questions.stem: Which OSPF area type blocks Type 5 external LSAs but still allows an ASBR within the area to inject externals as Type 7 LSAs?

explanation.correct: An NSSA blocks ordinary Type 5 externals but permits a local ASBR to originate Type 7 LSAs, which the ABR translates back into Type 5 for the rest of the OSPF domain.

distractors.A: A stub area blocks Type 5 and cannot contain an ASBR at all.
distractors.B: A totally stubby area blocks Type 5 AND Type 3, also no ASBR.
distractors.D: The backbone carries all LSA types and connects areas; it is not a stub variant.

explanation.exam_pattern: Stub=no Type5 (default route in). Totally stubby=no Type5/Type3. NSSA=no Type5 but Type7 allowed (ABR translates 7→5). Totally NSSA adds no Type3.

questions.stem: Which feature, enabled on an access port, will err-disable the port if it receives a superior BPDU, protecting a configured STP topology from a rogue switch?

explanation.correct: BPDU Guard err-disables a PortFast-enabled access port the moment it receives ANY BPDU — stopping a rogue switch from joining STP on that port.

distractors.A: Root Guard puts a port in root-inconsistent (blocking) state on a superior BPDU but does not err-disable it; it is used on designated ports facing other switches.
distractors.C: Loop Guard prevents a blocking port from erroneously moving to forwarding when BPDUs STOP arriving — a different failure mode.
distractors.D: UDLD detects unidirectional fiber links, not rogue BPDUs.

explanation.exam_pattern: BPDU Guard = any BPDU on PortFast port → err-disable. Root Guard = superior BPDU → root-inconsistent (recovers automatically). Loop Guard = missing BPDUs → loop-inconsistent.

questions.stem: An iBGP-learned prefix is in the BGP table but NOT installed in the routing table or advertised onward, and 'show ip bgp' shows it without a '>' best marker and flagged as inaccessible. What is the classic cause?

options.text: The BGP next-hop is not reachable via the IGP (next-hop unresolved)
The prefix has too short an AS-path

explanation.correct: iBGP does not change the next-hop by default, so if the IGP cannot reach that next-hop, the path is invalid and cannot become best. Fixing the IGP or using 'next-hop-self' resolves it.

distractors.B: A short AS-path would make a path MORE preferred, not invalid.
distractors.C: Synchronization is off by default on modern IOS and is unrelated to an unreachable next-hop.
distractors.D: High local-pref would make the path preferred, not inaccessible.

explanation.exam_pattern: iBGP next-hop stays the eBGP peer's address → must be IGP-reachable. Symptom: valid-but-not-best, 'inaccessible'. Fix: redistribute the link into IGP or 'neighbor x next-hop-self'.

questions.stem: Which QoS mechanism DROPS or RE-MARKS traffic that exceeds a configured rate (rather than buffering it), and is therefore better suited to high-speed interfaces where delay must stay low?

explanation.correct: Policing enforces a rate by dropping or re-marking excess traffic immediately — no queuing/delay. It can be applied inbound or outbound and produces a hard rate limit.

distractors.B: Shaping BUFFERS excess traffic to smooth it to the rate, adding delay; it is outbound only — the opposite trade-off.
distractors.C: WRED is a congestion-AVOIDANCE drop mechanism within queues, not a rate enforcer.
distractors.D: LLQ is a priority queuing method for real-time traffic, not a policer.

explanation.exam_pattern: Policing = drop/re-mark excess (no delay, in or out). Shaping = buffer excess (adds delay, outbound). WRED = selective drops to avoid tail drop. LLQ = strict priority queue.

questions.stem: To make all OSPF Gigabit and 10-Gig links show distinct costs, you set a network-wide OSPF reference bandwidth of 10 Gbps. Enter the exact router-ospf command (values in Mbps).

explanation.correct: 'auto-cost reference-bandwidth 10000' sets the reference to 10,000 Mbps (10 Gbps), so a 1 Gbps link gets cost 10 and a 10 Gbps link cost 1 — distinguishable instead of all flooring to 1.
explanation.exam_pattern: Reference bandwidth is in Mbps. Must be set identically on ALL routers or costs become inconsistent. Default is 100 (100 Mbps).

questions.stem: You must capture traffic from a source switch and deliver it to an analyzer attached to a DIFFERENT switch across the campus. Which feature is required?

options.text: A simple port mirror on the analyzer switch

explanation.correct: RSPAN carries mirrored traffic across switches using a dedicated RSPAN VLAN trunked between them, so the analyzer can sit on a different switch than the source.

distractors.A: Local SPAN only mirrors between ports on the SAME switch.
distractors.C: A local mirror on the analyzer switch cannot see traffic on the remote source switch.
distractors.D: NetFlow exports flow STATISTICS, not a full packet copy for analysis.

explanation.exam_pattern: Local SPAN=same switch. RSPAN=across switches via RSPAN VLAN. ERSPAN=across an L3/routed network via GRE. NetFlow=stats, not packets.

questions.stem: An IP SLA ICMP-echo operation is tracked and tied to a static default route so the route is withdrawn if the next hop stops responding. Which object links the SLA result to the route?

options.text: A 'track' object referencing the IP SLA, used in the ip route command
An EEM applet that deletes the route
A route-map with a match clause

explanation.correct: You create 'track <n> ip sla <id> reachability' and append the track to the static route ('ip route ... track <n>'). When the SLA fails, the track goes down and IOS removes the route.

distractors.B: An EEM applet could script it, but the standard, purpose-built mechanism is object tracking tied to IP SLA.
distractors.C: Route-maps filter/modify routes; they do not tie an SLA probe to a static route.
distractors.D: A prefix-list matches prefixes; it does not track reachability.

explanation.exam_pattern: IP SLA + object tracking + static route = reliable static routing/failover. 'ip route ... track N' is the glue. Often paired with a floating static backup.

references: ENCOR 350-401 Topic 4.2 IP SLA / object tracking

questions.stem: In Flexible NetFlow, which component defines WHICH key and non-key fields are collected for a flow (e.g., match source/destination IP, collect byte counts)?

explanation.correct: The flow record defines the fields: 'match' statements are the KEY fields that define a unique flow, and 'collect' statements are the non-key fields (counters/attributes) gathered.

distractors.B: The flow exporter defines WHERE flow data is sent (collector IP, port, version).
distractors.C: The flow monitor ties a record + exporter together and is applied to an interface.
distractors.D: A sampler reduces load by sampling 1-in-N packets; it does not define fields.

explanation.exam_pattern: FNF pieces: record (what: match=key, collect=non-key), exporter (where to send), monitor (binds record+exporter to interface), sampler (how often).

questions.stem: Which statement about SNMP vs model-driven telemetry (MDT) for network monitoring is correct?

options.text: SNMP pull-polls at intervals; streaming telemetry pushes data continuously based on subscriptions
SNMP pushes data continuously; telemetry only polls on request
Both require the collector to poll each OID individually every second

explanation.correct: Traditional SNMP is pull-based (the NMS polls OIDs periodically). Model-driven telemetry is push-based: the device streams data per a subscription (periodic or on-change), scaling better with less overhead.

distractors.B: This is reversed — SNMP polls, telemetry pushes.
distractors.C: Per-OID per-second polling is exactly the SNMP scalability problem telemetry solves.
distractors.D: MDT is built ON YANG models (via NETCONF/gRPC/gNMI); it absolutely uses them.

explanation.exam_pattern: SNMP = pull/poll, OID-based, higher overhead at scale. MDT = push/stream, YANG-based, periodic or on-change subscriptions (gRPC/gNMI).

questions.stem: Your NMS must be certain it received each SNMP notification from a router, even across a lossy WAN. Which notification type should the router send, and why?

options.text: SNMP inform, because the NMS acknowledges it and the router retransmits if no ack arrives
SNMP trap, because traps are acknowledged by the NMS
SNMP trap, because traps use TCP for guaranteed delivery
Syslog level 7, because debugging messages are always reliable

explanation.correct: An SNMP inform is acknowledged by the receiver; if the router gets no ack, it retransmits — giving reliable delivery at the cost of more memory and bandwidth. Ideal when losing a notification is unacceptable.

distractors.B: Traps are fire-and-forget: the NMS does NOT acknowledge them, so a dropped trap is simply lost.
distractors.C: Both traps and informs ride over UDP (162); traps do not use TCP.
distractors.D: Syslog over UDP 514 is also unacknowledged, and severity 7 just means more verbose messages, not reliability.

explanation.exam_pattern: Trap = unacknowledged, lightweight, can be lost. Inform = acknowledged + retransmitted, heavier but reliable. Both UDP/162; the 'must be sure it arrived' clue = inform.

questions.stem: Which Control Plane Policing (CoPP) use case best protects a router's CPU?

options.text: Rate-limiting traffic destined to the device's control plane (e.g., excessive SSH/SNMP/ICMP to the router itself)
Blocking all transit user data through the router

explanation.correct: CoPP applies a QoS policy to the control plane to rate-limit or drop traffic punted to the CPU (management, routing, exceptions), shielding the CPU from floods/DoS while leaving transit traffic in hardware.

distractors.B: CoPP protects the device's own CPU, not a tool to block all transit traffic.
distractors.C: Encryption of sessions is SSH/TLS, not CoPP's function.
distractors.D: CoPP does not load-balance; it polices control-plane-bound traffic.

explanation.exam_pattern: CoPP = protect the CPU/control plane with a policy-map applied under 'control-plane'. Classify management/routing/ICMP, then police. Transit data is unaffected.

questions.stem: Which protocol does a Cisco switch (authenticator) use to communicate with Cisco ISE (authentication server) in an 802.1X deployment, carrying the EAP exchange?

explanation.correct: 802.1X uses EAP over LAN (EAPoL) between supplicant and switch, and the switch relays EAP to the server inside RADIUS (EAP-over-RADIUS). ISE is a RADIUS server for authentication.

distractors.B: TACACS+ is used for device ADMINISTRATION AAA (command authorization), not 802.1X network access authentication.
distractors.C: LDAP may be an identity store ISE queries, but it is not the switch-to-ISE 802.1X transport.
distractors.D: Kerberos is not the 802.1X authenticator-to-server protocol.

explanation.exam_pattern: 802.1X: EAPoL (supplicant↔switch) + RADIUS (switch↔ISE). RADIUS=network access (UDP 1812/1813). TACACS+=device admin (TCP 49).

questions.stem: For administrative AAA, you need per-command authorization and full command accounting of what admins type on the CLI. Which protocol is the right choice and why?

options.text: TACACS+, because it separates AAA functions and supports per-command authorization
RADIUS, because it encrypts the entire packet
RADIUS, because it uses TCP for reliability

explanation.correct: TACACS+ separates authentication, authorization, and accounting, and supports granular per-command authorization — ideal for device admin. It runs over TCP 49 and encrypts the entire payload.

distractors.B: RADIUS encrypts only the password field, not the whole packet, and lumps authN/authZ together — weaker for per-command control.
distractors.C: SNMPv3 is for management data, not interactive admin command authorization.
distractors.D: RADIUS uses UDP, not TCP; the 'TCP reliability' claim actually describes TACACS+.

explanation.exam_pattern: TACACS+ = device admin (TCP 49, full encryption, per-command authZ, AAA separated). RADIUS = network access (UDP, password-only encryption, authN+authZ combined).

questions.stem: Which feature uses Security Group Tags (SGTs) to enforce policy based on group membership rather than IP addresses, decoupling policy from the network topology?

explanation.correct: Cisco TrustSec classifies traffic with Security Group Tags and enforces Security Group ACLs (SGACLs) based on group, so policy follows identity instead of IP/subnet.

distractors.B: Standard ACLs match source IP only — exactly the topology-coupled approach TrustSec replaces.
distractors.C: uRPF validates source addresses against the routing table (anti-spoofing), not group policy.
distractors.D: Port security limits MAC addresses on a port; it is not group-based policy.

explanation.exam_pattern: TrustSec = SGT classification + SGACL enforcement, policy by group not IP. Tags propagate inline (CMD) or via SXP. Often tied to ISE.

questions.stem: Which wireless security standard introduces SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) to replace the WPA2 pre-shared-key 4-way-handshake weaknesses?

explanation.correct: WPA3-Personal uses SAE (a.k.a. Dragonfly) for the handshake, providing forward secrecy and resistance to offline dictionary attacks that plagued WPA2-PSK.

distractors.B: WPA2-Enterprise uses 802.1X/EAP (not PSK) but still relies on the older handshake; SAE is a WPA3 feature.
distractors.C: WEP is the deprecated, broken legacy encryption (RC4) — the opposite of modern security.
distractors.D: Open authentication provides no encryption or authentication at all.

explanation.exam_pattern: WPA3-Personal = SAE (replaces PSK 4-way handshake, adds forward secrecy). WPA3-Enterprise = stronger 192-bit suite option. WEP/Open = insecure.

questions.stem: Which Embedded Event Manager (EEM) configuration will run a CLI action automatically when interface GigabitEthernet0/1 goes down?

options.text: A static 'ip sla' probe with no track

explanation.correct: EEM applets fire on events; a 'event syslog pattern' that matches the %LINK-3-UPDOWN down message for Gi0/1 triggers the applet, whose 'action' lines then run CLI (e.g., 'cli command'). 'event none' allows manual runs.

distractors.B: Route-maps filter routes; they cannot trigger actions on an interface event.
distractors.C: An IP SLA probe measures reachability but does not itself run CLI actions.
distractors.D: Prefix-lists match prefixes for routing policy, not event-driven scripting.

explanation.exam_pattern: EEM = event detector (syslog/snmp/timer/interface/none) + actions (cli/syslog/mail). Match on syslog patterns or track objects to automate reactions.

questions.stem: Which statement about YAML (as used in Ansible) is correct?

options.text: Indentation (spaces, not tabs) defines structure; lists use '- ' and maps use 'key: value'
YAML requires curly braces for every object like JSON
Tabs are the required indentation character in YAML

explanation.correct: YAML is whitespace-significant: consistent SPACE indentation defines hierarchy, '- ' denotes list items, and 'key: value' defines mappings. It is a superset of JSON but far more human-readable.

distractors.B: YAML does not require braces; flow style (braces) is optional, block style (indentation) is typical.
distractors.C: TABS are explicitly forbidden for indentation in YAML — a common breakage.
distractors.D: YAML represents arbitrarily nested maps and lists.

explanation.exam_pattern: YAML: spaces only (no tabs), '-' for list items, 'key: value' maps, indentation = hierarchy. JSON = braces/brackets. XML = tags. Know how each nests.

questions.stem: A NETCONF client must commit a change only if it validates, with the ability to roll back. Which NETCONF datastore feature supports this edit-then-commit workflow?

options.text: Writing directly to the running datastore only

explanation.correct: NETCONF's candidate datastore lets you stage edits, validate, then apply them atomically with <commit> (or throw them away with <discard-changes>), enabling safe, roll-back-able changes.

distractors.B: Editing running directly applies immediately with no staging/rollback window.
distractors.C: Startup is the saved boot config; TFTP is not a NETCONF commit workflow.
distractors.D: SNMP SET is not a NETCONF datastore operation and lacks this transactional model.

explanation.exam_pattern: NETCONF datastores: running (active), candidate (staging for commit), startup (boot). Candidate + <commit> = transactional config. RESTCONF lacks candidate/commit semantics.

questions.stem: In Python, you parse a RESTCONF JSON response into the variable 'data'. The interface list is at data['ietf-interfaces:interfaces']['interface']. What is the type of that value, and how do you get the first interface's name?

options.text: A string; use .split() to get the name
An integer index into a tuple
A set; use .pop() to read the name

explanation.correct: YANG 'interface' is a list, so JSON decodes it to a Python list of dicts. Index [0] gives the first dict, and ['name'] reads its name key.

distractors.B: It is structured data (list of objects), not a flat string to split.
distractors.C: JSON arrays map to Python lists, not tuples, and you index them by position.
distractors.D: JSON has no set type; arrays become ordered lists, not unordered sets.

explanation.exam_pattern: JSON→Python: object→dict, array→list, string→str, true/false→bool, null→None. Navigate nested data with ['key'] and [index].

questions.stem: A script authenticates to Cisco Catalyst Center (DNA Center) and receives a token to include in subsequent API calls. In which HTTP header is that token typically placed for later requests?

explanation.correct: Catalyst Center issues a token from POST /dna/system/api/v1/auth/token; clients send it back in the 'X-Auth-Token' header on subsequent REST calls to prove they are authenticated.

distractors.B: Content-Length describes the body size, not authentication.
distractors.C: User-Agent identifies the client software, not the auth token.
distractors.D: Host names the target server; it carries no credentials.

explanation.exam_pattern: Token-based REST auth: POST credentials → get token → send token in an auth header (X-Auth-Token for Catalyst Center; often 'Authorization: Bearer' elsewhere) on each call.

questions.stem: In a classic three-tier campus design, which layer is the Layer 3 aggregation point that applies policy and summarizes routes between the access layer and the core?

explanation.correct: The distribution layer aggregates access-layer switches, is the usual Layer 2/Layer 3 boundary, applies policy (ACLs/QoS), and summarizes routes toward the core.

distractors.B: The access layer connects end devices and enforces port-level features (PoE, port security), not route summarization.
distractors.C: The core is built for high-speed, low-latency transport and avoids policy to keep forwarding fast.
distractors.D: Spine is a data-center (spine-leaf) role, not the campus distribution layer.

explanation.exam_pattern: Access = connect hosts; Distribution = policy + L2/L3 boundary + summarization; Core = fast transport. A collapsed core merges core + distribution (two-tier).

questions.stem: A small campus uses a collapsed-core (two-tier) design. What does 'collapsed core' mean?

options.text: The core and distribution functions run on the same devices
The network uses a single switch for everything

explanation.correct: A collapsed-core (two-tier) design combines the core and distribution roles into the same distribution switches, which is cost-effective for small/medium campuses that don't need a dedicated core.

distractors.B: A collapsed core still uses Layer 3 at the distribution boundary.
distractors.C: The access layer remains; it's the core that is merged into distribution.
distractors.D: It's still a multi-switch design with redundancy, not one switch.

explanation.exam_pattern: Two-tier = collapsed core (core merged into distribution). Three-tier adds a dedicated core for large networks / many distribution blocks.

questions.stem: Which high-availability mechanism lets a redundant supervisor continue forwarding using the existing hardware (CEF) tables while the control plane restarts, avoiding a traffic outage?

explanation.correct: SSO synchronizes state to a standby supervisor so it takes over instantly, and NSF keeps forwarding from the existing CEF/FIB entries while routing protocols gracefully re-converge — so data traffic isn't dropped during a supervisor failover.

distractors.B: HSRP provides gateway redundancy between devices, not intra-chassis supervisor failover.
distractors.C: RSTP edge ports speed STP transitions, unrelated to supervisor redundancy.
distractors.D: PortFast is an access-port STP feature, not control-plane HA.

explanation.exam_pattern: NSF/SSO = control-plane HA within a chassis (keep forwarding during switchover). FHRP = gateway HA between chassis. Don't mix the two.

questions.stem: Which technology lets multiple physical Catalyst switches be managed and operate as a single logical switch over a dedicated ring, sharing one control plane?

explanation.correct: StackWise joins several access switches into one logical unit over a StackWise ring, with a single management/control plane and cross-stack EtherChannel — simplifying operations and adding redundancy.

distractors.B: VRRP is a first-hop gateway redundancy protocol, not switch stacking.
distractors.C: MST is a spanning-tree variant that maps VLANs to instances.
distractors.D: GLBP is a load-balancing FHRP, not a stacking technology.

explanation.exam_pattern: StackWise (access) and VSS/StackWise Virtual (distribution/core) = many boxes, one logical switch. FHRPs (HSRP/VRRP/GLBP) = gateway redundancy only.

questions.stem: In Cisco SD-Access, which protocols provide the fabric control plane and the fabric data plane, respectively?

options.text: LISP for the control plane and VXLAN for the data plane
OSPF for the control plane and GRE for the data plane
BGP for the control plane and MPLS for the data plane
STP for the control plane and 802.1Q for the data plane

explanation.correct: SD-Access uses LISP as the control plane (endpoint-ID to routing-locator mapping database), VXLAN as the data-plane encapsulation, and Cisco TrustSec (SGTs) for group-based policy.

distractors.B: OSPF/GRE describe a traditional routed overlay, not the SD-Access fabric planes.
distractors.C: BGP/MPLS is a service-provider VPN model, not the SD-Access fabric design.
distractors.D: STP/802.1Q is classic Layer 2, which the fabric overlay specifically replaces.

explanation.exam_pattern: SD-Access = LISP (control) + VXLAN (data) + TrustSec/SGT (policy). Underlay is any routed IP transport (often IS-IS).

questions.stem: In an SD-Access fabric, which node is responsible for connecting the fabric to networks outside of it (e.g., the data center or WAN)?

explanation.correct: The fabric border node is the gateway between the fabric and external domains (WAN, data center, Internet), handling route import/export and the hand-off of fabric traffic.

distractors.B: The fabric edge node connects endpoints (like an access switch) into the fabric.
distractors.C: The control-plane node runs the LISP map-server/resolver (endpoint database).
distractors.D: Intermediate nodes are pure underlay transport (no fabric role).

explanation.exam_pattern: Roles: edge = connect endpoints; border = exit to external; control-plane = LISP map database; intermediate = underlay transit.

questions.stem: A client moves between two lightweight APs joined to the SAME WLC and keeps its IP address. What type of roam is this?

explanation.correct: When both APs are on the same WLC, the controller simply updates its client database — an intra-controller (Layer 2) roam — and the client keeps its IP with minimal disruption.

distractors.B: Inter-controller roaming involves two different WLCs (Layer 2 or Layer 3 mobility between them).
distractors.C: Auto-anchor tunnels guest traffic to a DMZ anchor controller — a specific design, not this basic same-WLC roam.
distractors.D: There is no 'mobility-group reset' roam type.

explanation.exam_pattern: Same WLC = intra-controller roam. Different WLCs = inter-controller (L2 if same client subnet, L3 if different, using anchor/foreign).

questions.stem: In Cisco DNA Center Assurance, what is the primary role of its AI/ML analytics?

options.text: Establish behavioral baselines and flag anomalies/issues with guided remediation
Replace the routing protocol on every device
Encrypt all management traffic end to end
Act as the DHCP server for the fabric

explanation.correct: DNA Center Assurance uses machine learning to build baselines of normal network/client behavior, detect anomalies and correlate them into issues, and suggest or automate remediation — shifting ops from reactive to proactive.

distractors.B: Analytics observe and advise; they don't replace routing protocols.
distractors.C: Encrypting management traffic is a security feature, not the purpose of ML analytics.
distractors.D: DHCP services are unrelated to the assurance analytics engine.

explanation.exam_pattern: Network AI/ML (DNA Assurance) = baselining + anomaly detection + guided remediation. Think 'insight and automation,' not forwarding.

questions.stem: Which description best matches 'supervised' machine learning as applied to network analytics?

options.text: A model trained on labeled examples to predict/classify new data
A model that finds structure in unlabeled data via clustering
A static rule set written by an engineer
A protocol that floods telemetry to all collectors

explanation.correct: Supervised learning trains on labeled input/output pairs so the model can classify or predict outcomes for new, unseen data (e.g., 'this traffic pattern = this application').

distractors.B: Finding structure in UNlabeled data via clustering is UNsupervised learning.
distractors.C: A hand-written rule set is not machine learning at all.
distractors.D: That describes a telemetry transport mechanism, not an ML method.

explanation.exam_pattern: Supervised = labeled data → predict/classify. Unsupervised = unlabeled → cluster/anomaly. Know the one-line distinction.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a Type 1 hypervisor from a Type 2 hypervisor?

options.text: Type 1 runs directly on the server hardware (bare-metal); Type 2 runs on top of a host OS
Type 1 runs on top of a host OS; Type 2 runs on bare metal
Type 1 only runs containers; Type 2 only runs VMs

explanation.correct: A Type 1 (bare-metal) hypervisor such as ESXi runs directly on hardware for best performance and isolation. A Type 2 hypervisor (e.g., VirtualBox) runs as an application on top of a host operating system.

distractors.B: Reversed — Type 1 is bare-metal, Type 2 is hosted.
distractors.C: Both types virtualize full VMs; containers are a separate OS-level virtualization model.
distractors.D: The placement (bare-metal vs hosted) is a real, exam-relevant difference.

explanation.exam_pattern: Type 1 = bare-metal (ESXi, KVM, Hyper-V role). Type 2 = hosted on an OS (VirtualBox, VMware Workstation). Containers share the host kernel.

questions.stem: How do containers differ from virtual machines?

options.text: Containers share the host OS kernel and package only the app + dependencies; VMs include a full guest OS
Containers each include a full guest operating system
VMs are always smaller and faster to start than containers
Containers require a Type 1 hypervisor to run

explanation.correct: Containers virtualize at the OS level: they share the host kernel and bundle just the application and its libraries, so they're lightweight and start quickly. VMs virtualize hardware and each carry a complete guest OS.

distractors.B: Carrying a full guest OS describes a VM, not a container.
distractors.C: Containers are generally smaller and faster to start than VMs, not the reverse.
distractors.D: Containers use a container runtime on the host OS, not a hypervisor.

explanation.exam_pattern: Container = share kernel, app+libs, fast/light. VM = full guest OS on a hypervisor, stronger isolation, heavier.

questions.stem: What does VRF-lite provide on a single router?

options.text: Multiple independent routing/forwarding tables for traffic segmentation
Automatic IP address assignment to hosts

explanation.correct: VRF (Virtual Routing and Forwarding) creates multiple isolated routing and forwarding tables on one device, so overlapping or separate customer/segment traffic stays logically separated. 'VRF-lite' is VRF without MPLS.

distractors.B: VRF segments routing; it does not encrypt packets (that's IPsec/MACsec).
distractors.C: VRF is a logical construct, not hardware supervisor redundancy.
distractors.D: Address assignment is DHCP, unrelated to VRF.

explanation.exam_pattern: VRF = separate routing tables per segment on one box. VRF-lite = no MPLS; full MPLS L3VPN adds RD/RT with MP-BGP.

questions.stem: How many Layer 2 segments can VXLAN identify, and what field provides that scale compared with a traditional VLAN?

explanation.correct: VXLAN uses a 24-bit VNID (VNI), giving ~16 million segments — far beyond the 4094 usable VLANs of the 12-bit 802.1Q ID. VXLAN encapsulates Ethernet in UDP (port 4789) between VTEPs.

distractors.B: 4096 (12-bit) is the traditional VLAN limit VXLAN was created to exceed.
distractors.C: 16 bits (65,536) is not the VXLAN VNI size.
distractors.D: 8 bits is unrelated to VXLAN.

explanation.exam_pattern: VXLAN: 24-bit VNI (~16M segments), MAC-in-UDP (4789), VTEP endpoints, often MP-BGP EVPN control plane. VLAN = 12-bit (4094).

questions.stem: In a VXLAN overlay, what is the function of a VTEP?

options.text: It encapsulates/decapsulates Ethernet frames into/out of VXLAN at the edge
It is the underlay routing protocol
It is the controller that assigns VNIs

explanation.correct: A VTEP (VXLAN Tunnel Endpoint) sits at the edge of the overlay and performs encapsulation of local Ethernet frames into VXLAN/UDP toward remote VTEPs, and decapsulation in the reverse direction.

distractors.B: The 24-bit identifier is the VNI, not the VTEP.
distractors.C: The underlay runs normal IP routing; the VTEP uses it but isn't the routing protocol.
distractors.D: A controller (or MP-BGP EVPN) handles mappings; the VTEP does the encap/decap.

explanation.exam_pattern: VTEP = encap/decap edge. VNI = segment ID. Underlay = IP transport. EVPN/controller = control plane/mapping.

questions.stem: A point-to-point GRE tunnel is configured between two routers across the Internet. By itself, what does GRE provide?

options.text: Tunneling of multiple protocols with NO native encryption
Strong AES encryption of the payload
Built-in dynamic routing without any routing protocol

explanation.correct: GRE encapsulates many passenger protocols (including multicast/routing updates) in an IP tunnel, but it provides NO encryption on its own — it is commonly paired with IPsec for confidentiality.

distractors.B: GRE does not encrypt; add IPsec for that.
distractors.C: GRE is not MPLS labeling.
distractors.D: GRE carries routing protocols but doesn't replace them; you still run OSPF/EIGRP/BGP over it.

explanation.exam_pattern: GRE = flexible multiprotocol/multicast tunnel, no crypto. GRE-over-IPsec adds encryption. DMVPN builds on mGRE + IPsec + NHRP.

questions.stem: Which OSPF LSA type is generated by an ABR to advertise a network from one area into another (inter-area route)?

explanation.correct: A Type 3 Summary LSA is originated by an Area Border Router to advertise networks learned in one area into other areas (inter-area/O IA routes).

distractors.B: Type 1 Router LSAs describe a router's links WITHIN an area; they don't cross area boundaries.
distractors.C: Type 5 External LSAs carry routes redistributed from outside OSPF (via an ASBR), shown as O E1/E2.
distractors.D: Type 2 Network LSAs are generated by the DR to describe a multi-access segment within an area.

explanation.exam_pattern: LSA cheat sheet: 1 Router, 2 Network (DR), 3 Summary (ABR inter-area), 4 ASBR-summary, 5 External (ASBR), 7 NSSA-external.

questions.stem: In a totally stubby area, which routes does the ABR inject, and what is blocked?

options.text: Only a default route is injected; both Type 5 external and Type 3 inter-area LSAs are blocked
All external and inter-area routes are allowed
Only Type 5 externals are allowed; inter-area is blocked
Nothing is injected; the area is isolated

explanation.correct: A totally stubby area blocks both Type 5 (external) and Type 3 (summary/inter-area) LSAs; the ABR injects a single default route (0.0.0.0/0) so internal routers reach everything through the ABR — minimizing LSDB size.

distractors.B: A regular (non-stub) area allows all; this is specifically a totally stubby area.
distractors.C: Stub areas block Type 5 but still allow Type 3; totally stubby blocks both.
distractors.D: The area isn't isolated — it reaches the rest via the injected default.

explanation.exam_pattern: Stub: block Type 5 (default in). Totally stubby: block Type 5 + 3 (default in). NSSA: allow Type 7 externals. Totally NSSA: Type 7 + default, block 3/5.

questions.stem: Two BGP routers are stuck in the 'Active' state and never reach Established. What does 'Active' most commonly indicate?

options.text: The router is trying to initiate a TCP session but is not getting a reply (reachability/peer problem)
The session is up and actively exchanging routes
The neighbor relationship is fully established

explanation.correct: In BGP, 'Active' means the router is actively trying to open the TCP (port 179) session to the peer but not succeeding — usually a reachability issue, wrong neighbor IP, missing route to the peer, an ACL, or a mismatched remote-AS/update-source.

distractors.B: Exchanging routes happens only in the ESTABLISHED state.
distractors.C: 'Active' is a session FSM state, not a traffic-forwarding behavior.
distractors.D: Established — not Active — is the fully formed peering state.

explanation.exam_pattern: BGP FSM: Idle→Connect→Active→OpenSent→OpenConfirm→Established. Stuck in Active/Idle = TCP 179 reachability/config problem.

questions.stem: Ignoring Weight, which BGP path attribute is evaluated FIRST in best-path selection, and is it higher-or-lower-preferred?

options.text: Origin code — IGP over EGP over incomplete

explanation.correct: After the Cisco-only Weight (highest, local to the router), the next attribute is Local Preference, where HIGHER wins. It is exchanged among iBGP peers to influence the AS's egress choice.

distractors.B: MED is far down the list and only compared (lowest wins) between paths from the same neighboring AS.
distractors.C: AS-Path (shortest wins) is evaluated after Local Preference and locally originated checks.
distractors.D: Origin (IGP<EGP<incomplete) comes after AS-Path and origin-type checks.

explanation.exam_pattern: Order (mnemonic 'We Love Oranges AS Oranges Mean Pure Refreshment'): Weight↑, LocalPref↑, Originated-local, AS-path↓, Origin(IGP), MED↓, eBGP>iBGP, lowest IGP metric, router-id.

questions.stem: An iBGP-learned route has a next hop that other iBGP routers can't reach, so the route is not used. Which command on the border router fixes this cleanly?

explanation.correct: By default BGP does not change the next hop on iBGP-advertised eBGP routes, so internal routers may not have a route to that external next hop. 'next-hop-self' makes the border router advertise itself as the next hop, which internal routers can always reach.

distractors.B: ebgp-multihop is for forming eBGP sessions between non-directly-connected peers, not fixing the iBGP next hop.
distractors.C: always-compare-med changes MED comparison, unrelated to next-hop reachability.
distractors.D: remove-private-as strips private ASNs on eBGP advertisements, not the next-hop issue.

explanation.exam_pattern: iBGP next-hop-unreachable → 'next-hop-self' on the border router (or advertise the external subnet into the IGP). Classic iBGP gotcha.

questions.stem: In EIGRP, a route's Feasible Distance is 3072 via the successor. A second path has a Reported (advertised) Distance of 2560 and a computed distance of 4096. Is that second path a feasible successor?

options.text: Yes — its RD (2560) is less than the FD (3072), satisfying the feasibility condition
No — its total computed distance (4096) is greater than the FD
No — EIGRP has no feasible successors

explanation.correct: The feasibility condition tests the neighbor's Reported Distance against the current Feasible Distance: if RD < FD, the path is loop-free and qualifies as a feasible successor (a precomputed backup). 2560 < 3072, so yes — even though its own total distance is higher.

distractors.B: The feasibility test uses the REPORTED distance, not the total computed distance, so 4096 doesn't disqualify it.
distractors.C: The comparison is RD < FD, not total > FD.
distractors.D: EIGRP absolutely uses feasible successors (loop-free backups) via DUAL.

explanation.exam_pattern: Feasibility condition: neighbor's RD < my FD → feasible successor (instant backup). Successor = lowest FD. If no FS, DUAL goes Active and queries.

questions.stem: By default (K1=K3=1, others 0), EIGRP's composite metric is based on which two path characteristics?

explanation.correct: With default K-values (K1=1, K3=1, K2=K4=K5=0), EIGRP's metric uses the minimum bandwidth along the path and the cumulative delay. MTU is carried but not used in the metric.

distractors.B: Hop count is RIP's metric; MTU is not part of the EIGRP metric calculation.
distractors.C: Reliability and load are only used if you enable K2/K4/K5 (not recommended, can cause instability).
distractors.D: MTU is tracked (tie-break/info) but is not a metric component.

explanation.exam_pattern: Default EIGRP metric = bandwidth (min) + delay (sum). K2/K4/K5 off. Changing K-values must match on all neighbors or adjacency fails.

questions.stem: Which protocol do IPv4 hosts use to tell their local router which multicast groups they want to receive?

explanation.correct: IGMP (Internet Group Management Protocol) runs between hosts and their first-hop router so hosts can join/leave IPv4 multicast groups. The router then uses PIM upstream to build the distribution tree.

distractors.B: PIM builds multicast trees BETWEEN routers; it isn't the host-to-router signaling.
distractors.C: CGMP is a legacy Cisco switch/router protocol, largely replaced by IGMP snooping.
distractors.D: MSDP shares source info between PIM-SM domains (RPs), not host membership.

explanation.exam_pattern: Host↔router = IGMP (v2 most common; v3 adds source filtering). Router↔router trees = PIM (sparse uses an RP + shared tree, then source tree).

questions.stem: In PIM Sparse Mode, what is the role of the Rendezvous Point (RP)?

options.text: It is the root of the shared tree where sources and receivers initially meet
It floods multicast to every router and prunes back
It is the receiver's default gateway
It assigns multicast group addresses to hosts

explanation.correct: PIM-SM is pull-based: the RP is the root of the shared (*,G) tree. Sources register to the RP and receivers join toward it, so they 'meet' at the RP; routers may then build a shortest-path (S,G) source tree and cut over to it.

distractors.B: Flood-and-prune is PIM DENSE mode behavior, not sparse mode with an RP.
distractors.C: The RP is a multicast tree root, not a unicast default gateway.
distractors.D: Group addresses aren't assigned to hosts by the RP; apps choose group addresses.

explanation.exam_pattern: PIM-SM = RP-rooted shared tree (*,G), then switch to source tree (S,G) via RPF. PIM-DM = flood-and-prune. RPF check prevents loops.

questions.stem: In MST (802.1s), two switches must be in the same MST region to interoperate as one instance. Which THREE attributes must match to form a region?

options.text: Region name, revision number, and VLAN-to-instance mapping
Bridge priority, root cost, and port roles
Hostname, management IP, and NTP server

explanation.correct: Switches are in the same MST region only if their configuration name, revision number, and VLAN-to-instance mapping are identical. A mismatch in any one puts the switch in a different region (boundary behavior).

distractors.B: Those are STP election outcomes, not the region-membership criteria.
distractors.C: Hostname/IP/NTP are unrelated to MST region identity.
distractors.D: VTP is a VLAN distribution protocol, separate from MST region membership.

explanation.exam_pattern: MST region = same NAME + REVISION + VLAN-to-instance MAP. Any difference = separate region. MST maps many VLANs onto few instances.

questions.stem: You want a Layer 3 (routed) EtherChannel between two switches. Which sequence is correct on the port-channel interface?

options.text: 'no switchport' then 'ip address ...' on the port-channel, with members set to the same channel-group
Assign the IP to each physical member individually

explanation.correct: A routed EtherChannel is created by making the port-channel a Layer 3 interface: 'no switchport' then assign the 'ip address'. The physical members join via 'channel-group N mode ...' and must also be 'no switchport'.

distractors.B: 'switchport mode trunk' keeps it Layer 2; you can't put an IP on a switchport.
distractors.C: The IP belongs on the port-channel logical interface, not on each member.
distractors.D: Access-VLAN config is Layer 2; it conflicts with routing an IP on the channel.

explanation.exam_pattern: L3 EtherChannel: 'no switchport' + ip address on Port-channel; members 'no switchport' + channel-group. L2 EtherChannel uses switchport trunk/access.

questions.stem: In the Modular QoS CLI (MQC), what is the correct build order to apply a policy to an interface?

options.text: class-map (match) → policy-map (action) → service-policy on the interface

explanation.correct: MQC: define a class-map to MATCH traffic, reference it in a policy-map to set the ACTION (mark/queue/police/shape), then attach the policy to an interface with service-policy input|output.

distractors.B: The class-map must exist before the policy-map references it.
distractors.C: service-policy is the last step (applies the finished policy), not the first.
distractors.D: route-maps are for PBR/redistribution, not the standard MQC QoS flow.

explanation.exam_pattern: MQC = class-map (match) → policy-map (do) → service-policy (apply). Match first, act second, attach last.

questions.stem: Which queuing feature guarantees low latency for voice by servicing a priority queue first, up to a policed bandwidth?

explanation.correct: LLQ adds a strict-priority queue (policed to a configured bandwidth) on top of CBWFQ, so real-time voice is dequeued first for minimal latency and jitter while the policer prevents it from starving other classes.

distractors.B: WRED is a congestion-AVOIDANCE drop mechanism, not a low-latency queue.
distractors.C: Plain WFQ fairly shares bandwidth but offers no strict priority for voice.
distractors.D: FIFO gives no differentiation at all.

explanation.exam_pattern: LLQ = CBWFQ + strict priority (policed) for voice/real-time. WRED = avoid congestion via early random drops. Shaping buffers; policing drops.

questions.stem: OSPFv3 for IPv6 differs from OSPFv2 in which key way regarding how it enables the protocol on interfaces?

options.text: OSPFv3 is enabled per-interface (e.g., 'ipv6 ospf 1 area 0'), not via network statements
OSPFv3 uses the same 'network' area statements as OSPFv2
OSPFv3 runs only on loopback interfaces
OSPFv3 requires a 32-bit router-id derived from an IPv6 address

explanation.correct: OSPFv3 is configured per-interface with 'ipv6 ospf <pid> area <area>' (or the newer address-family model), rather than the OSPFv2 'network ... area' statements under the router process.

distractors.B: OSPFv3 does NOT use 'network' statements; that's the OSPFv2 method.
distractors.C: OSPFv3 runs on any participating interface, not only loopbacks.
distractors.D: OSPFv3 still uses a 32-bit router-id, but it must be configured manually if no IPv4 is present — and that's not the 'how it's enabled' difference asked.

explanation.exam_pattern: OSPFv3: per-interface enablement, runs over IPv6 link-local, still 32-bit RID (set it if no IPv4), uses LSAs 8/9 for link/prefix info.

questions.stem: Which feature forwards packets based on a policy (e.g., source address or application) instead of the normal destination-based routing table?

explanation.correct: PBR uses a route-map (often matching an ACL on source/app) with 'set ip next-hop' to override the normal destination-based forwarding — useful for sending specific traffic over a particular path.

distractors.B: CEF is the fast-switching forwarding architecture; it follows the routing table, it doesn't apply policy.
distractors.C: ECMP load-shares across equal-cost destination routes; it's still destination-based.
distractors.D: GLBP is a first-hop redundancy/load-balancing protocol, not source-based forwarding.

explanation.exam_pattern: PBR = route-map + match (ACL) + set next-hop, applied inbound with 'ip policy route-map'. Overrides destination routing for matched traffic.

questions.stem: What is the administrative distance of an eBGP route versus an iBGP route on a Cisco router?

explanation.correct: Cisco assigns eBGP an administrative distance of 20 (very trusted, beating IGPs) and iBGP 200 (less trusted than IGPs like OSPF/EIGRP), so internal IGP routes are usually preferred over iBGP for the same prefix.

distractors.B: Reversed — eBGP is the low (20) one.
distractors.C: 110 is OSPF, not BGP.
distractors.D: 90/170 are internal/external EIGRP.

explanation.exam_pattern: AD: eBGP 20, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, IS-IS 115, RIP 120, ext-EIGRP 170, iBGP 200. eBGP's low AD can override IGPs — watch for that.

questions.stem: Which RSTP port role is a backup path to the root that is normally discarding and takes over if the root port fails?

explanation.correct: In RSTP, the alternate port provides an alternate path to the root bridge; it is discarding during normal operation and can rapidly become the root port if the current root port is lost.

distractors.B: A designated port is the forwarding port for a segment (away from root).
distractors.C: The root port is the active best path to the root — the one being backed up.
distractors.D: A backup port is a redundant link to the SAME segment (seen with hubs), not an alternate path to the root.

explanation.exam_pattern: RSTP roles: Root (best to root), Designated (forward per segment), Alternate (backup path to root, discarding), Backup (redundant to same segment).

questions.stem: Which IPv4 multicast range is reserved for link-local control traffic (e.g., OSPF 224.0.0.5/.6, EIGRP 224.0.0.10) and is never routed?

explanation.correct: 224.0.0.0–224.0.0.255 (224.0.0.0/24) is the link-local scope used by control protocols (OSPF 224.0.0.5/6, EIGRP 224.0.0.10, RIPv2 224.0.0.9). Routers do not forward this range (TTL effectively 1).

distractors.B: 232.0.0.0/8 is Source-Specific Multicast (SSM).
distractors.C: 239.0.0.0/8 is the administratively-scoped/private multicast range.
distractors.D: 233.0.0.0/8 is GLOP addressing.

explanation.exam_pattern: 224.0.0.0/24 = link-local control (not routed). 232/8 = SSM. 239/8 = private/org-local. Memorize the protocol group addresses.

questions.stem: You need to copy traffic from switches in a remote closet to an analyzer several hops away across a routed Layer 3 network. Which SPAN technology is required?

explanation.correct: ERSPAN encapsulates mirrored traffic in GRE so it can be routed across a Layer 3 network to a remote analyzer — exactly the multi-hop, routed requirement here.

distractors.B: Local SPAN only mirrors between ports on the SAME switch.
distractors.C: RSPAN carries mirrored traffic over a special VLAN across switches, but that VLAN must be trunked Layer 2 end to end — it can't traverse a routed L3 network.
distractors.D: A hub is not a management-grade solution and doesn't solve the L3 transport problem.

explanation.exam_pattern: Local SPAN = same switch. RSPAN = across switches via an L2 VLAN. ERSPAN = across an L3/routed network via GRE.

questions.stem: In Flexible NetFlow, what determines whether two packets belong to the SAME flow?

options.text: They match on all of the flow record's KEY fields (match statements)
They share the same non-key (collect) fields
They are exported by the same flow exporter
They arrive on the same SNMP ifIndex only

explanation.correct: A Flexible NetFlow flow is defined by the KEY fields (the 'match' statements in the flow record) — e.g., source/dest IP, ports, protocol, ToS. Packets identical on all key fields are the same flow; 'collect' (non-key) fields just add data like byte/packet counts.

distractors.B: Non-key (collect) fields are gathered per flow but don't define flow identity.
distractors.C: The exporter sends the data to a collector; it doesn't define flows.
distractors.D: Interface index alone doesn't define a flow; the full key set does.

explanation.exam_pattern: FNF pieces: flow RECORD (match=key, collect=non-key) → flow MONITOR (record + cache) → flow EXPORTER (where to send). Key fields define the flow.

questions.stem: How is IP SLA typically used to drive automatic failover of a static default route?

options.text: An IP SLA probe is tied to a tracked object; the static route is conditioned on 'track', and withdrawn if the probe fails
IP SLA directly edits the routing table on failure
IP SLA increases OSPF cost automatically
IP SLA sends a RADIUS message to reroute

explanation.correct: You configure an IP SLA probe (e.g., icmp-echo to a target), bind it to a tracked object, and add 'track' to the static route. If the probe fails, the tracked object goes down and the static route is withdrawn, letting a floating backup route take over.

distractors.B: IP SLA doesn't edit routes directly; object tracking + the route's 'track' keyword does the conditioning.
distractors.C: IP SLA doesn't auto-adjust OSPF cost; that's a different mechanism.
distractors.D: RADIUS is unrelated to IP SLA route failover.

explanation.exam_pattern: IP SLA + track + static route = reachability-based failover. Probe down → tracked object down → route withdrawn → backup installs.

references: ENCOR 350-401 Topic 4.x IP SLA + object tracking

questions.stem: To see 'debug' output in an SSH/VTY session (not just the console), which command must you run in that session?

explanation.correct: Debug and log messages go to the console by default. In a VTY (Telnet/SSH) session you must enter 'terminal monitor' to mirror logging/debug output to that remote session.

distractors.B: 'logging console' affects the console line, not your remote VTY session.
distractors.C: 'debug all' is dangerous (can overload the CPU) and still wouldn't appear in your VTY without terminal monitor.
distractors.D: 'show logging' displays the buffer once; it doesn't stream live debugs to your session.

explanation.exam_pattern: Remote session + want live debugs = 'terminal monitor'. Be sparing with debugs on production (CPU impact); prefer conditional debugging.

questions.stem: Which SNMPv3 security level provides BOTH authentication and encryption of the SNMP payload?

explanation.correct: SNMPv3 'authPriv' authenticates the sender (HMAC-MD5/SHA) AND encrypts the payload (DES/AES) for confidentiality — the most secure level.

distractors.B: authNoPriv authenticates but does NOT encrypt.
distractors.C: noAuthNoPriv provides neither (community-string-like).
distractors.D: 'privNoAuth' is not a valid level — you can't have privacy without auth.

explanation.exam_pattern: SNMPv3 levels: noAuthNoPriv < authNoPriv < authPriv. Privacy (encryption) always requires authentication, so authPriv is the top.

questions.stem: A traceroute shows '* * *' for one hop but completes to the destination on later hops. What is the MOST likely explanation?

options.text: That hop is not replying to the probes (e.g., ICMP/TTL-exceeded rate-limited or filtered), but still forwards traffic
There is a routing loop at that hop
DNS resolution failed for the whole path

explanation.correct: A single hop of '* * *' that still lets the trace complete means that router isn't sending TTL-exceeded/port-unreachable replies (filtered or rate-limited control-plane responses), yet it continues to forward the data plane normally.

distractors.B: If the destination were unreachable the trace wouldn't complete to it.
distractors.C: A loop would show repeating addresses and the trace wouldn't progress cleanly to the end.
distractors.D: DNS only affects name display; numeric hops would still show.

explanation.exam_pattern: Intermittent '*' at one hop but trace completes = that hop isn't answering probes (filtered/rate-limited control plane), not a data-plane failure.

questions.stem: Which three components must be assembled and applied to an interface to collect and export Flexible NetFlow data?

options.text: A flow record, a flow exporter, and a flow monitor
A class-map, a policy-map, and a service-policy
An ACL, a route-map, and a prefix-list
A SPAN source, a SPAN destination, and a VLAN

explanation.correct: FNF is built from a flow RECORD (which fields/keys to track), a flow EXPORTER (where to send the data), and a flow MONITOR (ties the record + cache + exporter) that is applied to the interface with 'ip flow monitor'.

distractors.B: class-map/policy-map/service-policy is the QoS (MQC) flow, not NetFlow.
distractors.C: ACL/route-map/prefix-list are routing/policy constructs, not NetFlow.
distractors.D: Those are SPAN components, a different monitoring feature.

explanation.exam_pattern: FNF = record + exporter + monitor, applied to the interface. Record = what; exporter = where; monitor = glue + apply.

questions.stem: Which IP SLA operation is specifically designed to measure one-way latency, jitter, and packet loss for VoIP-style traffic?

explanation.correct: The IP SLA udp-jitter operation sends timestamped UDP packets to a responder, measuring jitter, latency (including one-way with time sync), and loss — the metrics that matter for voice/video.

distractors.B: icmp-echo measures round-trip reachability/latency but not jitter.
distractors.C: tcp-connect measures connection setup time to a TCP port.
distractors.D: The dns operation measures name-resolution time.

explanation.exam_pattern: udp-jitter = jitter/latency/loss (VoIP), needs an IP SLA Responder. icmp-echo = basic reachability. Pick by the metric required.

questions.stem: Which command shows the real-time CPU utilization and the processes consuming it on an IOS device?

explanation.correct: 'show processes cpu' (optionally 'sorted' or 'history') displays overall CPU utilization for 5s/1m/5m and a per-process breakdown — the go-to for diagnosing a high-CPU condition.

distractors.B: 'show memory' reports memory allocation, not CPU.
distractors.C: 'show version' shows image/uptime/hardware, not live CPU.
distractors.D: 'show ip interface brief' lists interface status/IPs.

explanation.exam_pattern: High CPU? → 'show processes cpu sorted'. High memory? → 'show processes memory'. Know which 'show' answers which symptom.

questions.stem: Which AAA protocol is preferred for DEVICE ADMINISTRATION because it separates authentication, authorization, and accounting and encrypts the entire packet?

explanation.correct: TACACS+ (TCP 49, Cisco-originated) encrypts the whole payload and splits AAA into independent functions, which makes it ideal for per-command authorization during device administration.

distractors.B: RADIUS (UDP) encrypts only the password and combines auth+authz; it's preferred for network ACCESS (802.1X), not granular device admin.
distractors.C: SNMPv2c is a management protocol with weak community-string security, not AAA.
distractors.D: Kerberos is a ticket-based auth system, not the device-admin AAA transport described.

explanation.exam_pattern: Device admin (per-command authz, full encryption) → TACACS+. Network access (802.1X) → RADIUS. Match use case to protocol.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of Control Plane Policing (CoPP)?

options.text: Rate-limit/filter traffic destined to the router's control plane (CPU) to protect it from overload/DoS

explanation.correct: CoPP applies a QoS policy to traffic punted to the control plane (the CPU) — e.g., routing protocols, SSH, SNMP, ARP — so excessive or malicious control traffic is policed/dropped and the CPU stays protected during a storm or DoS.

distractors.B: Encrypting routing updates is authentication/MACsec, not CoPP.
distractors.C: Load-balancing is a data-plane/forwarding function, unrelated to CoPP.
distractors.D: SGT assignment is TrustSec, a separate feature.

explanation.exam_pattern: CoPP = protect the CPU/control plane with a policed service-policy on 'control-plane'. Classify control traffic, then police/drop excess.

questions.stem: Which authentication method does WPA3-Personal use to replace the WPA2-Personal 4-way handshake and resist offline dictionary attacks?

explanation.correct: WPA3-Personal uses SAE (a.k.a. Dragonfly), which provides forward secrecy and resists offline dictionary attacks against the pre-shared password, replacing the WPA2-PSK method.

distractors.B: TKIP is the deprecated WPA/legacy cipher, not WPA3's authentication.
distractors.C: WEP shared key is obsolete and insecure.
distractors.D: EAP-TLS is an 802.1X enterprise method (certificates); the question is about WPA3-PERSONAL, which uses SAE.

explanation.exam_pattern: WPA3-Personal = SAE (anti-dictionary, forward secrecy). WPA3-Enterprise = 802.1X/EAP + optional 192-bit mode. WPA2-Personal = PSK 4-way handshake.

questions.stem: A printer without an 802.1X supplicant must still be authenticated on a secured switch port. Which feature authenticates it by its MAC address?

explanation.correct: MAB lets the switch send the device's MAC address to the RADIUS server (ISE) as the identity when no 802.1X supplicant responds, so headless devices like printers can be authorized. It's commonly a fallback after 802.1X times out.

distractors.B: EAP-FAST is an 802.1X EAP method requiring a supplicant — which the printer lacks.
distractors.C: Web auth needs a user with a browser to enter credentials — not suitable for a printer.
distractors.D: Port security limits MACs locally but does NOT authenticate against a central policy server (no dynamic authorization/dACL/SGT).

explanation.exam_pattern: Headless device on a dot1x port → MAB (MAC as identity to RADIUS). Order often: 802.1X → MAB → WebAuth as fallbacks.

questions.stem: Which feature drops packets that arrive with a source IP that the router would not use that interface to reach (anti-spoofing based on the FIB)?

explanation.correct: uRPF checks the source address of incoming packets against the FIB: in strict mode, if the best route back to that source isn't via the ingress interface, the packet is dropped — mitigating IP spoofing.

distractors.B: DHCP snooping validates DHCP messages and builds the binding table; it isn't FIB-based source validation.
distractors.C: DAI validates ARP against the DHCP snooping bindings (Layer 2), not the routing FIB.
distractors.D: Storm control rate-limits broadcast/multicast/unicast floods, not spoofed sources.

explanation.exam_pattern: uRPF = FIB-based source check (strict vs loose) for anti-spoofing. Layer 2 anti-spoofing = DHCP snooping + DAI + IP Source Guard.

questions.stem: Which configuration restricts VTY (SSH) management access to only the subnet 10.10.10.0/24?

options.text: An access-class ACL applied to the VTY lines permitting 10.10.10.0 0.0.0.255
login local on the console line

explanation.correct: Management-plane access is restricted by applying an ACL to the VTY lines with 'access-class <acl> in'. Permitting only 10.10.10.0/24 limits who can open an SSH/Telnet session to the device.

distractors.B: 'ip access-group' filters transit/data traffic on an interface, not who can log in to the VTY lines.
distractors.C: service password-encryption obfuscates stored passwords; it doesn't restrict source access.
distractors.D: 'login local' sets the auth method on the console, not a source-IP restriction on VTY.

explanation.exam_pattern: Restrict management logins → 'access-class' on 'line vty'. Restrict transit traffic → 'ip access-group' on the interface. Don't swap them.

questions.stem: Which planes are being referred to when hardening a router for 'management plane, control plane, and data plane' protection?

options.text: Managing the device (SSH/SNMP), running protocols/CPU traffic, and forwarding user packets

explanation.correct: The management plane handles device administration (SSH, SNMP, NetConf); the control plane runs protocols and processes CPU-punted traffic (routing, ARP); the data plane forwards user traffic. Each is hardened with different tools (e.g., VTY ACLs, CoPP, infrastructure ACLs/uRPF).

distractors.B: Physical/virtual/cloud are deployment layers, not the three device planes.
distractors.C: Access/distribution/core are campus tiers, not device planes.
distractors.D: North/south/east-west describe traffic directions, not device planes.

explanation.exam_pattern: Management = admin access (VTY ACL, AAA, SSH). Control = CPU/protocols (CoPP, routing auth). Data = forwarding (iACLs, uRPF, DAI/IPSG).

questions.stem: On a WLC, which WLAN security option uses an external RADIUS server and 802.1X/EAP to authenticate each wireless user individually?

explanation.correct: WPA2/WPA3-Enterprise uses 802.1X with an external RADIUS/AAA server so each user authenticates with unique credentials (or certificates) via EAP — unlike a single shared PSK.

distractors.B: WPA2-Personal uses one shared pre-shared key for everyone, no per-user RADIUS auth.
distractors.C: Open authentication provides no authentication at all.
distractors.D: Static WEP is obsolete and insecure.

explanation.exam_pattern: Per-user auth with RADIUS = Enterprise/802.1X/EAP. Shared password = Personal/PSK. WPA3 strengthens both (SAE / 192-bit).

questions.stem: In Cisco TrustSec, how is policy enforced independently of IP addressing?

options.text: Traffic is tagged with a Security Group Tag (SGT) and filtered by an SGACL based on group, not IP
By applying a standard numbered ACL per subnet
By assigning each user a static VLAN only

explanation.correct: TrustSec classifies endpoints into security groups and carries a Security Group Tag (SGT) with their traffic; SGACLs then permit/deny based on source/destination GROUP, decoupling policy from IP addresses and subnets.

distractors.B: Per-subnet numbered ACLs are exactly the IP-coupled approach TrustSec avoids.
distractors.C: Static VLAN assignment alone isn't group-based policy enforcement.
distractors.D: DHCP reservations assign addresses; they don't enforce group policy.

explanation.exam_pattern: TrustSec = classify → tag (SGT) → enforce (SGACL) by group. Policy follows identity/group, not IP/subnet.

questions.stem: Which command set is the minimum to force SSH (and disable Telnet) for remote management on the VTY lines?

options.text: transport input ssh (on line vty), plus a hostname, ip domain-name, and crypto key generate rsa
transport input telnet on line vty

explanation.correct: SSH needs an RSA key pair, which requires a hostname and ip domain-name before 'crypto key generate rsa'. Restricting the VTY lines with 'transport input ssh' then forces SSH and blocks Telnet.

distractors.B: 'transport input telnet' allows the insecure protocol — the opposite of the goal.
distractors.C: Password encryption alone doesn't enable SSH or block Telnet.
distractors.D: 'enable secret' protects privileged mode but doesn't configure SSH transport.

explanation.exam_pattern: SSH recipe: hostname + ip domain-name + crypto key generate rsa (≥768-bit, 2048 recommended) + 'transport input ssh' + local/AAA login.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of an infrastructure ACL (iACL) deployed at the network edge?

options.text: Protect the infrastructure IP space by denying external traffic TO device addresses while permitting transit traffic THROUGH
Replace routing protocols with static filtering

explanation.correct: An iACL permits legitimate transit traffic through the network but denies packets destined to the infrastructure's own device/loopback addresses from untrusted sources, shielding routers from direct attack.

distractors.B: iACLs filter; they don't encrypt.
distractors.C: iACLs complement routing; they don't replace it.
distractors.D: QoS marking is a separate function from an infrastructure protection ACL.

explanation.exam_pattern: iACL = deny-to-infrastructure, permit-through. Protects device addresses at the edge; pair with CoPP (control plane) and uRPF (anti-spoof).

questions.stem: What is the key advantage of model-driven telemetry (MDT) over traditional SNMP polling for operational data?

options.text: Devices PUSH data via subscriptions (periodic or on-change), which scales better and is more real-time than pull-based polling
It uses UDP community strings for authentication
It requires the NMS to poll each OID individually

explanation.correct: MDT lets the device stream YANG-modeled data to a collector on a subscription (periodic intervals or on-change), typically over gRPC/gNMI or NETCONF. Push + structured data scales far better and is more timely than SNMP's per-OID polling.

distractors.B: Community strings are SNMP; MDT uses modern transports/security (gRPC/TLS).
distractors.C: Per-OID polling is exactly the SNMP limitation MDT replaces.
distractors.D: MDT uses gRPC/gNMI/NETCONF over secure transports, not Telnet.
